arXiv:2405.19428v2 [math.AP] 08 Sep 2025

The spreading of global solutions of chemotaxis systems with logistic source and consumption on ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}

Zulaihat Hassan Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Statistics    Wenxian Shen Affiliation: Auburn University, Auburn, AL 36849    Yuming Paul Zhang Affiliation: U.S.A.
Abstract

This paper investigates the spreading properties of globally defined bounded positive solutions of a chemotaxis system featuring a logistic source and consumption:

{∂tu=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+u(a−bu),(t,x)∈(0,∞)×ℝN,τ∂tv=Δv−uv,(t,x)∈(0,∞)×ℝN,\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}u=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+u(a-bu),\quad&(t,x)\in{(0},\infty)\times\mathbb{R}^{N},\\ &{\tau\partial_{t}v}=\Delta v-uv,\quad&(t,x)\in{(0},\infty)\times\mathbb{R}^{N},\end{aligned}\right.

where uu represents the population density of a biological species, and vv denotes the density of a chemical substance. We show that the presence of the chemical does not hinder the spreading of the species in general, and it does not accelerate the spreading speed under conditions that v⁡(0,⋅)v(0,\cdot) decays spatially or the parameters satisfy 0<−χ≪10<-\chi\ll 1 and τ=1\tau=1. In the proof, we establish a novel connection between uu and vv using the sup- and inf-convolution techniques for viscosity solutions. Additionally, our numerical simulations reveal a noteworthy phase transition in χ\chi: for v⁡(0,⋅)v(0,\cdot) uniformly distributed across space, the spreading speed accelerates only when χ\chi surpasses a critical positive value.

Keywords: Chemotaxis systems, logistic source, consumption, spreading speed

AMS Subject Classification (2020): 35B40, 35K57, 35Q92, 92C17

1 Introduction

The current paper is devoted to the study of the asymptotic behavior of globally defined bounded solutions of the following parabolic-parabolic chemotaxis system with logistic source and consumption

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+u(a−bu),(t,x)∈(0,∞)×ℝN,τvt=Δv−uv,(t,x)∈(0,∞)×ℝN,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+u(a-bu),\quad&(t,x)\in{(0},\infty)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\\ {\tau v_{t}}=\Delta v-uv,\quad&(t,x)\in{(0},\infty)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\end{cases} (1.1)

where χ\chi is a constant that can be either positive or negative, and aa, bb, and τ\tau are positive constants. In (1.1), u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) denotes the population density of some biological species and v⁡(t,x)v(t,x) denotes the population density of some chemical substance at time tt and space location xx; χ\chi is referred to as the chemotaxis sensitivity coefficient; the reaction term u⁡(a−b​u)u(a-bu) is referred to as a logistic source; and τ\tau is linked to the diffusion rate of the chemical substance. The chemotaxis sensitivity coefficient χ>0\chi>0 indicates that the biological species is being attracted by the chemical signal, and χ<0\chi<0 indicates that the biological species is repelled by the chemical signal.

Chemotaxis is a phenomenon in which the movement of living organisms or cells is partially oriented along the gradient of certain chemicals. This phenomenon plays an important role in many biological processes, such as embryo formation and tumor development. The development of mathematical models for chemotaxis dates back to the pioneering works of Keller and Segel in the 1970s ([22, 23, 24]). Since these pioneering works, a large amount of research has been carried out on various chemotaxis models. See, for example, [18, 19, 21, 33, 42, 47], etc. for the study of global existence and finite-time blow-up in the following minimal chemotaxis model on a bounded domain,

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v),x∈Ω,τvt=Δu+g(u,v)−h(u,v)v,x∈Ω,∂u∂n=∂v∂n=0,x∈∂Ω,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v),\quad&x\in\Omega,\cr\tau v_{t}=\Delta u+g(u,v)-h(u,v)v,\quad&x\in\Omega,\cr\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial n}=0,\quad&x\in\partial\Omega,\end{cases} (1.2)

where Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{N} is a smooth bounded domain.

Before diving into a more detailed discussion of this problem and the history of past developments, let us briefly describe the main theoretical results of the paper for the benefit of the readers. Firstly, we show a lower bound for spreading speeds of solutions to (1.1) with general non-negative initial data u0u_{0} in Theorem 1.1. This lower bound equals the spreading speed when χ=0\chi=0, that is, when chemotaxis is absent. Theorem 1.2 states that the chemical substance does not induce infinitely fast spreading of uu and vv. Finally, we prove that the upper bound of the spreading speed is the same as the lower bound, showing no acceleration due to chemotaxis, under certain conditions: when v⁡(0,⋅)v(0,\cdot) decays in space (see Theorem 1.3(1)), and when 0<−χ≪10<-\chi\ll 1 and τ=1\tau=1 (see Theorem 1.3(2)).

Let us highlight the proof of Theorem 1.3(2), where we uncover a novel connection between the population densities of the species uu and the chemical substance vv. Specifically, we introduce the variables ζ:=1−v\zeta:=1-v and

w:=ζp/u for some ​p>1,w:=\zeta^{p}/u\qquad\text{ for some }p>1,

and we show that, under the conditions of the theorem, ww is uniformly finite in both space and time after a short initial period. For more details, we refer the readers to the discussion in Remark 1.3 (4) and Lemma 5.3.

Now, we discuss the existing literature on (1.2). In [42, 47], (1.2) was considered with τ=1\tau=1, g⁡(u,v)=0g(u,v)=0, h⁡(u,v)=uh(u,v)=u and this model is referred to as chemotaxis model with consumption. It is proved in [42, Theorem 1.1] that this equation has a unique globally defined bounded classical solution with non-negative initial functions (u0,v0)∈(W1,p​(Ω))2(u_{0},v_{0})\in(W^{1,p}(\Omega))^{2} for some p>Np>N provided that

0<‖v0‖L∞​(Ω)⋅χ<16​(N+1).0<\|v_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\cdot\chi<\frac{1}{6(N+1)}. (1.3)

The authors in [47] proved that any globally defined bounded positive classical solutions of (1.2) converge to (1|Ω|​∫Ωu0,0)(\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}u_{0},0) as t→∞t\to\infty. In [18, 19, 21, 33], (1.2) is studied with g⁡(u,v)=μ​u,g(u,v)=\mu u, and h⁡(u,v)=λh(u,v)=\lambda (OPENμ,λ>0).\mu,\lambda>0). It is known that finite-time blow-up does not occur when N=1N=1 and may occur when N≥2N\geq 2 (see [19], [33], etc.).

We refer the reader to [20, 29, 34, 35, 44, 46, 48], etc. for the study of the following chemotaxis model with a logistic source on a bounded domain,

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+u(a−bu),x∈Ω,τvt=Δu+g(u,v)−h(u,v)v,x∈Ω,∂u∂n=∂v∂n=0,x∈∂Ω.\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+u(a-bu),\quad&x\in\Omega,\cr\tau v_{t}=\Delta u+g(u,v)-h(u,v)v,\quad&x\in\Omega,\cr\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial n}=0,\quad&x\in\partial\Omega.\end{cases} (1.4)

Assume τ=1,\tau=1, g⁡(u,v)=0,g(u,v)=0, and h⁡(u,v)=uh(u,v)=u. It is proved in [44, Theorem 3.3] that (1.4) has a unique globally defined bounded classical solution with non-negative initial functions (u0,v0)∈(W1,p​(Ω))2(u_{0},v_{0})\in(W^{1,p}(\Omega))^{2} for some p>Np>N, provided that (1.3) holds. It is also proved in [29] that this equation has a unique globally defined bounded classical solution with non-negative initial (u0,v0)∈(C⁡(Ω¯)×C1​(Ω¯))(u_{0},v_{0})\in(C(\bar{\Omega})\times C^{1}(\bar{\Omega})) provided that χ​‖v0‖L∞​(Ω)\chi\|v_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)} is small relative to bb (see [29, Theorem 1.1]), and that any positive bounded globally defined classical solution converges to (ab,0)(\frac{a}{b},0) as t→∞t\to\infty (see [29, Theorem 1.2]). Furthermore, if τ=1,g⁡(u,v)=μ​u,\tau=1,g(u,v)=\mu u, and h⁡(u,v)=λh(u,v)=\lambda, it is known (see [20, 46]) that finite-time blow-up does not occur provided

b>N​|χ|​μ/4.b>{N|\chi|\mu}/{4}.

The study of chemotaxis models on the whole space can provide some deep insight into the influence of chemotaxis on the evolution of biological species from some different angles. For instance, it can help determine whether chemotaxis would speed up or slow down the invasion of the biological species. Also, there have been numerous studies investigating chemotaxis models on the entire space. For instance, refer to [5, 12, 13, 15, 16, 30, 31, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41, 45], etc. for investigations into the following chemotaxis model:

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+u(a−bu),x∈ℝN,τ​vt=Δ​v−λ​v+μ​u,x∈ℝN,u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x),v⁡(0,x)=v0​(x)x∈ℝN.\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+u(a-bu),&x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\\ {\tau v_{t}}=\Delta v-\lambda v+\mu u,&x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\\ u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\,\,v(0,x)=v_{0}(x)&x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}.\end{cases} (1.5)

Observe that, in the absence of chemotaxis (i.e., χ=0\chi=0), the dynamic of (1.5) is governed by the following reaction-diffusion equation,

ut=Δ​u+u⁡(a−b​u),x∈ℝN.u_{t}=\Delta u+u(a-bu),\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}. (1.6)

The equation is also known as Fisher-KPP equation due to the pioneering works of Fisher [8] and Kolmogorov, Petrowsky, Piskunov [27] on traveling wave solutions and take-over properties. The spreading properties of (1.6) are well-established. Equation (1.6) has traveling wave solutions u⁡(t,x)=ϕ⁡(x⋅ξ−c​t)u(t,x)=\phi(x\cdot\xi-ct) (ξ∈𝕊N−1\xi\in\mathbb{S}^{N-1}) connecting ab\frac{a}{b} and 00 (ϕ⁡(−∞)=ab,ϕ⁡(∞)=0)(\phi(-\infty)=\frac{a}{b},\phi(\infty)=0) for all speeds c≥2​ac\geq 2\sqrt{a} and there is no such traveling wave solutions of slower speeds. For any given bounded u0∈C⁡(ℝN,ℝ+)u_{0}\in C({\mathbb{R}}^{N},{\mathbb{R}}^{+}) with nonempty compact support,

limt→∞sup|x|≤c′​t|u⁡(t,x)−ab|=0∀c′<2​a,\lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_{|x|\leq c^{\prime}t}\left|u(t,x)-\frac{a}{b}\right|=0\quad\forall\,c^{\prime}<2\sqrt{a}, (1.7)

and

limt→∞sup|x|≥c′′​tu⁡(t,x)=0∀c′′>2​a\lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_{|x|\geq c^{\prime\prime}t}u(t,x)=0\quad\forall\,c^{\prime\prime}>2\sqrt{a} (1.8)

(see [2, 3]). Thanks to (1.7) and (1.8), in literature, the minimal wave speed c∗:=2​ac^{*}:=2\sqrt{a} is also called the spreading speed of (1.6).

Considering (1.5), it is an important question whether the chemotaxis speeds up or slows down the spreading of the biological species. When τ=1\tau=1, it is proved in [41] that if b>N​χ​μ4,b>\frac{N\chi\mu}{4}, chemotaxis neither speed up nor slow down the spreading speed of the biological species in the sense that (1.7) and (1.8) hold for any solution (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))(u(t,x),v(t,x)) of (1.5) with initial data (u0​(⋅),v0​(⋅))(u_{0}(\cdot),v_{0}(\cdot)) whose supports are nonempty and compact. When τ=0\tau=0, it is proved in [40] that if b>χ​μb>\chi\mu and (1+(a−λ)+2​(a+λ))​χ​μ≤b,\big(1+\frac{(\sqrt{a}-\sqrt{\lambda})_{+}}{2(\sqrt{a}+\sqrt{\lambda})}\big)\chi\mu\leq b, then again chemotaxis neither slows down nor speeds up the spreading speed. Assuming τ=0\tau=0 and N=1N=1, the authors of [12] proved that negative chemotaxis speeds up the spatial spreading of the biological species in the sense that the minimal wave speed of traveling waves of (1.5) must be greater than c∗=2​ac^{*}=2\sqrt{a} when −χ-\chi is sufficiently large.

Very recently, the authors of the current paper studied the global existence of the chemotaxis models (1.1) and (1.5) in a unified way. Sufficient conditions are provided for positive classical solutions to exist globally and stay bounded (see [14, Theorems 1.2-1.4]. In this paper, we focus on the study of asymptotic behavior of globally defined bounded solutions of (1.1), specially, spreading speeds of globally defined bounded positive solutions of (1.1).

In the following, we introduce some notations and definitions in subsection 1.1, state our main theoretical results, and discuss novel ideas and techniques in subsection 1.2, and present some numerical observations in subsection 1.3.

1.1 Notations and definitions

In this subsection, we introduce some standing notations and the definition of spreading speeds. Let us define

X:=Cunifb​(ℝN)={u∈C⁡(ℝN)|u⁡(x)​is uniformly continuous in​x∈ℝN​and​supx∈ℝN|u⁡(x)|<∞}X:=C_{\rm unif}^{b}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})=\big\{u\in C({\mathbb{R}}^{N})\,|\,u(x)\,\,\text{is uniformly continuous in}\,\,x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\,\,{\rm and}\,\,\sup_{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}|u(x)|<\infty\big\}

equipped with the norm ‖u‖∞:=supx∈ℝN|u⁡(x)|\|u\|_{\infty}:=\sup_{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}|u(x)|. We also set

X+:={u∈X|u≥0},X^{+}:=\{u\in X\,|\,u\geq 0\},

and

Xc+:={u∈X+|supp(u)≠∅,supp(u)is compact}.X_{c}^{+}:=\big\{u\in X^{+}\,|\,{\rm supp}(u)\not=\emptyset,\,\,{\rm supp}(u)\,\,\text{is compact}\big\}.

Next, we let

X1:=Cunif1,b(ℝN)={u∈X|∂u∂xi∈Xfori=1,2,⋯,N}X_{1}:=C_{\rm unif}^{1,b}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})=\left\{u\in X\,\big|\,\frac{\partial u}{\partial x_{i}}\in X\,\,{\rm for}\,\,i=1,2,\cdots,N\right\}

equipped with the norm ‖u‖X1:=‖u‖∞+∑i=1N‖∂u∂xi‖∞\|u\|_{X_{1}}:=\|u\|_{\infty}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|\frac{\partial u}{\partial x_{i}}\|_{\infty}. We write X1+:=X1∩X+X_{1}^{+}:=X_{1}\cap X^{+}. Finally, we use Cunif2+α,b​(ℝN)C_{\rm unif}^{2+\alpha,b}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}) to denote all u∈X1u\in X_{1} such that ∂2u∂xi​∂xj\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial x_{i}\partial x_{j}} are uniformly bounded and α\alpha-Hölder continuous for i,j=1,2,…,Ni,j=1,2,\ldots,N, and use the notation

C0​(ℝN):={u∈C⁡(ℝN)|lim|x|→∞u⁡(x)=0}.C_{0}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}):=\left\{u\in C({\mathbb{R}}^{N})\,\big|\,\lim_{|x|\to\infty}u(x)=0\right\}.

For any given (u0,v0)∈X+×X1+(u_{0},v_{0})\in X^{+}\times X_{1}^{+}, we denote by (u⁡(t,x,u0,v0),v⁡(t,x,u0,v0))(u(t,x;u_{0},v_{0}),v(t,x;u_{0},v_{0})) the classical solution of (1.1) satisfying

limt→0+(‖u⁡(t,⋅,u0,v0)−u0​(⋅)‖X+‖v⁡(t,⋅,u0,v0)−v0​(⋅)‖X1)=0,\lim_{t\to 0+}(\|u(t,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0})-u_{0}(\cdot)\|_{X}+\|v(t,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0})-v_{0}(\cdot)\|_{X_{1}})=0,
u⁡(⋅,⋅,u0,v0)∈C⁡([0,Tmax),X)∩C1​((0,Tmax),X),u(\cdot,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0})\in C([0,T_{\max}),X)\cap C^{1}((0,T_{\max}),X),
v⁡(⋅,⋅,u0,v0)∈C⁡([0,Tmax),X1)∩C1​((0,Tmax),X1).v(\cdot,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0})\in C([0,T_{\max}),X_{1})\cap C^{1}((0,T_{\max}),X_{1}).

Note that, by the comparison principle for parabolic equations, for every (u0,v0)∈X+×X1+(u_{0},v_{0})\in X^{+}\times X_{1}^{+}, it always holds that u⁡(t,x,u0,v0)≥0u(t,x;u_{0},v_{0})\geq 0 and v⁡(t,x,u0,v0)≥0v(t,x;u_{0},v_{0})\geq 0 for all t>0t>0 in the existence interval of the solution.

The objective of this paper is to study the asymptotic behavior of globally defined positive solutions. We introduce the following definitions. For given (u0,v0)∈X+×X1+(u_{0},v_{0})\in X^{+}\times X_{1}^{+}, assuming that (u⁡(t,x,u0,v0),v⁡(t,x,u0,v0))(u(t,x;u_{0},v_{0}),v(t,x;u_{0},v_{0})) exists for all t>0t>0, let

Slow(u0,v0):={c|c>0,lim inft→∞inf|x|≤c​tu(t,x;u0,v0)>0}S_{\rm low}(u_{0},v_{0}):=\{c\,|\,c>0,\,\,\liminf_{t\to\infty}\inf_{|x|\leq ct}u(t,x;u_{0},v_{0})>0\}

and

Sup(u0,v0):={c|c>0,lim supt→∞sup|x|≥c​tu(t,x;u0,v0)=0}.S_{\rm up}(u_{0},v_{0}):=\{c\,|\,c>0,\,\,\limsup_{t\to\infty}\sup_{|x|\geq ct}u(t,x;u_{0},v_{0})=0\}.

We define

clow∗​(u0,v0):=sup{c|c∈Slow​(u0,v0)}c_{\rm low}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0}):=\sup\{c\,|\,c\in S_{\rm low}(u_{0},v_{0})\}

and

cup∗​(u0,v0):=inf{c|c∈Sup​(u0,v0)},c_{\rm up}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0}):=\inf\{c|\,c\in S_{\rm up}(u_{0},v_{0})\},

where clow∗​(u0,v0)=0c_{\rm low}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0})=0 if Slow​(u0,v0)=∅S_{\rm low}(u_{0},v_{0})=\emptyset and cup∗​(u0,v0)=∞c_{\rm up}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0})=\infty if Sup​(u0,v0)=∅S_{\rm up}(u_{0},v_{0})=\emptyset. By the definition of clow∗​(u0,v0)c_{\rm low}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0}) and cup∗​(u0,v0)c_{\rm up}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0}), if clow∗​(u0,v0)>0c_{\rm low}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0})>0, then

lim inft→∞inf|x|≤c′​tu⁡(t,x,u0,v0)>0∀ 0<c′<clow∗​(u0,v0),\liminf_{t\to\infty}\inf_{|x|\leq{c^{\prime}}t}u(t,x;u_{0},v_{0})>0\quad\forall\,0<{c^{\prime}}<c^{*}_{\rm low}(u_{0},v_{0}),

and if cup∗​(u0,v0)<∞c_{\rm up}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0})<\infty, then

limt→∞sup|x|≥c′′​tu⁡(t,x,u0,v0)=0∀c′′>cup∗​(u0,v0).\lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_{|x|\geq{c^{\prime\prime}}t}u(t,x;u_{0},v_{0})=0\quad\forall\,{c^{\prime\prime}}>c^{*}_{\rm up}(u_{0},v_{0}).

If clow∗​(u0,v0)=cup∗​(u0,v0)c_{\rm low}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0})=c_{\rm up}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0}), then c∗​(u0,v0):=clow∗​(u0,v0)c^{*}(u_{0},v_{0}):=c_{\rm low}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0}) is called the spreading speed of the solution (u⁡(t,x,u0,v0),v⁡(t,x,u0,v0))(u(t,x;u_{0},v_{0}),v(t,x;u_{0},v_{0})). It is well known that when χ=0\chi=0, we have clow∗​(u0,v0)=cup∗​(u0,v0)=2​ac_{\rm low}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0})=c_{\rm up}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0})=2\sqrt{a} for any u0∈Xc+u_{0}\in X_{c}^{+} and v0∈X1+v_{0}\in X_{1}^{+} (see [2, 3]).

Many interesting questions arise when χ≠0\chi\not=0. For example, whether clow∗​(u0,v0)c_{\rm low}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0}) is positive and cup∗​(u0,v0)c_{\rm up}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0}) is finite; whether clow∗​(u0,v0)≥2​ac_{\rm low}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0})\geq 2\sqrt{a}, in other words, whether the chemotaxis does not slow down the population’s spreading; whether cup∗​(u0,v0)≤2​ac_{\rm up}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0})\leq 2\sqrt{a}, that is, whether the chemotaxis does not speed up the population’s spreading; whether clow∗​(u0,v0)=cup∗​(u0,v0)c_{\rm low}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0})=c_{\rm up}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0}), that is, the population has a single spreading speed; in the case clow∗​(u0,v0)>0c_{\rm low}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0})>0, whether u⁡(t,x,u0,v0)u(t,x;u_{0},v_{0}) converges to ab\frac{a}{b} in the region |x|<c​t|x|<ct for any 0<c<clow∗​(u0,v0)0<c<c_{\rm low}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0}), which is strongly related to the stability of the constant equilibrium (ab,0)(\frac{a}{b},0); and how χ\chi affects the spreading properties; etc. The goal of this paper is to answer some of these questions.

1.2 Main results, biological interpretations, and techniques

In this subsection, we state our main results on the asymptotic behavior of globally defined positive solutions, give some biological interpretations of the results, and highlight the techniques employed/developed in the proofs of the results.

Our first main result provides a lower bound of the spatial spreading speeds of solutions to (1.1) with general non-negative initial data u0u_{0}.

Theorem 1.1 (Lower bound of spreading speeds).

Suppose that u0∈X+u_{0}\in X^{+} and v0∈X1+v_{0}\in X^{+}_{1}, and (u⁡(t,x,u0,v0),v⁡(t,x,u0,v0))(u(t,x;u_{0},v_{0}),v(t,x;u_{0},v_{0})) is a globally defined bounded solution of (1.1). Remark 1.1.
  • (1)

    As it is mentioned in the above, when χ=0\chi=0, clow∗​(u0,v0)=2​ac_{\rm low}^{*}(u_{0},v_{0})=2\sqrt{a} for any u0∈Xc+u_{0}\in X_{c}^{+} and v0∈X1+v_{0}\in X_{1}^{+} (in this case, u⁡(t,x,u0,v0)u(t,x;u_{0},v_{0}) is independent of v0v_{0}). Note that, when χ<0\chi<0, the chemical substance is a chemorepellent, and when χ>0\chi>0, the chemical substance is a chemoattractant. Theorem 1.1 reveals an important biological observation: chemical substance does not slow down the propagation of the biological species with nonzero initial distribution even when the chemical substance is a chemorepellent.

  • (2)

    (1.9) is proved by nontrivially modified arguments of [41, Theorem 1.2(1)]. The key idea is to show that, for any given 0<c′<2​a0<c^{\prime}<2\sqrt{a}, u⁡(t,x+c​ξ​t,u0,v0)u(t,x+c\xi t;u_{0},v_{0}) is bounded away from zero uniformly in 0<c<c′0<c<c^{\prime}, ξ∈𝕊N−1\xi\in\mathbb{S}^{N-1}, |x|≤l|x|\leq l for some l>0l>0, and t≫1t\gg 1 (see Lemmas 3.1, 3.2, and 3.3). In the proof, we make use of special Harnack inequalities for bounded solutions of (1.1) established in Lemmas 2.3 and 2.4. Specifically, the local-in-time Harnack inequality, as stated in Lemma 2.3, is a slight generalization of [4, Theorem 1.2] and [13, Lemma 2.2], which address advection Fisher-KPP equations. Additionally, our approach employs the principal eigenvalue and eigenfunction of some linearized operator for uu, and the comparison principal for parabolic equations.

Remark 1.3.
  • (1)

    Note that the biological species gradually consumes the chemical substance over time. Consequently, if initially, the chemical substance does not occupy the entire space to a certain extent, as indicated by conditions such as v0∈Lp​(ℝN)v_{0}\in L^{p}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}) for some p≥1p\geq 1 or v0∈C0​(ℝN)v_{0}\in C_{0}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}), it intuitively follows that the spreading of the species should be unaffected. This intuition aligns with the findings of Theorem 1.3 (1).

  • (2)

    Recall that when χ<0\chi<0 (resp. χ>0\chi>0), the chemical substance acts as a chemorepellent (resp. chemoattractant). If v0v_{0} is not negligible as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty, it is reasonable to expect that negative chemotaxis wouldn’t enhance the spread of the biological species, while a chemoattractant might accelerate it. This expectation is partly supported by our Theorem 1.3 (2) when χ<0\chi<0 but |χ|≪1|\chi|\ll 1. However, the situation regarding chemoattractants is more complicated. Indeed, as confirmed by numerical simulations (refer to Section 6), a phase transition emerges: there exists a critical threshold, denoted as χ∗>0\chi^{*}>0, such that the spread accelerates when χ>χ∗\chi>\chi^{*}, while it maintains a constant speed of 2​a2\sqrt{a} when χ<χ∗\chi<\chi^{*}. Although Theorem 1.4 provides another evidence, the problem remains open.

  • (3)

    The additional smooth assumption u0∈X1+u_{0}\in X^{+}_{1} and v0∈Cunif2+α,b​(ℝN)v_{0}\in C_{\rm unif}^{2+\alpha,b}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}) guarantees the boundedness of ‖∇u​(t,⋅,u0,v0)‖∞\|\nabla u(t,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0})\|_{\infty} and ‖Δ​v​(t,⋅,u0,v0)‖∞\|\Delta v(t,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0})\|_{\infty} up to t=0t=0, which is a technical assumption used in our proof.

  • (4)

    To establish Theorem 1.3(2) and Theorem 1.4, we explore a novel connection between the population densities of the species uu and the chemical substance vv. Specifically, we introduce the variables ζ:=1−v\zeta:=1-v and

    w:=ζp/u for some ​p>1,w:=\zeta^{p}/u\qquad\text{ for some }p>1,

    and ww turns out to satisfy a favorable parabolic equation, see the proof of Lemma 5.3. Leveraging the smoothing effect inherent in the parabolic equation, we are able to show ζp≲u\zeta^{p}\lesssim u which leads to the estimates of ζ\zeta and ∇ζ\nabla\zeta in terms of u1/pu^{{1}/{p}}. However, a significant difficulty arises in this approach: since u0u_{0} and ζ0:=1−v0\zeta_{0}:=1-v_{0} are known to have compact support only, ww is not well-defined at time 00. To circumvent this obstacle, we prove that ζp≲u\zeta^{p}\lesssim u at some small positive times by using the comparison principle and employing the inf- and sup- convolution technique for viscosity solutions. Having ww be finite over at least a small positive time interval, we propagate this property to all subsequent times through the parabolic equation satisfied by ww. Linking the two density variables uu and vv is essential in the analysis of spreading properties.

1.3 Numerical simulations and biological indications

As mentioned before, numerical experiments indicate a phase transition, that is there exists a positive critical value of χ\chi, beyond which the spreading speed accelerates, while it remains to be 2​a2\sqrt{a} when χ<χ∗\chi<\chi^{*}. Theorem 1.3(2) confirmed this expectation for χ<0\chi<0 but |χ|≪1|\chi|\ll 1. We further compare the behavior of solutions for different values of τ\tau. We choose τ=0.5\tau=0.5 and τ=4.\tau=4. The result of the simulation shows that for large positive χ\chi, chemotaxis speeds up the spreading of the biological species for these τ\tau.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we present some preliminary materials for use in later sections, including a review of the global existence of classical solutions of (1.1); special Harnack inequalities for bounded solutions of (1.1); the comparison principle for viscosity solutions to general parabolic type equations; and convergence of globally defined bounded solutions of (1.1) to the constant solution (ab,0)(\frac{a}{b},0). Section 3 is devoted to the investigation of the lower bounds of spreading speeds of global bounded solutions of (1.1) and the proof of Theorem 1.1. In Section 4, we study the upper bounds of spreading speeds of global bounded solutions to (1.1) and prove Theorem 1.2. The existence of spreading speeds is discussed in Section 5. Theorems 1.3 and 1.4 are proved in this section. In Section 6, we present our numerical experiments. Finally, we give a proof of Lemma 2.3 in the appendix.

2 Preliminary

In this section, we recall some results from [14] about global existence and C1+θ,2+νC^{1+\theta,2+\nu}–boundedness of classical solutions of (1.1), present a Harnack type inequality for (1.1), and introduce the concept of viscosity solutions of general parabolic type equations and recall the comparison principle for viscosity solutions.

Remark 2.1.

It follows from Proposition 2.1 that the classical solution (u⁡(t,x,u0,v0)𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸(u(t,x;u_{0},v_{0}), 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁v⁡(t,x,u0,v0))v(t,x;u_{0},v_{0})) to (1.1) exists globally when |χ||\chi| is sufficiently small. Moreover, from its proof, we have that supt≥0‖u⁡(t,⋅,u0,v0)‖∞\sup_{t\geq 0}\|u(t,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0})\|_{\infty} stays uniformly finite for all small |χ||\chi|. We recall [14, Proposition 2.1(1)] about local existence of solutions: For any given u0∈Xu_{0}\in X and v0∈X1v_{0}\in X_{1}, there is Tmax:=Tmax​(u0,v0)∈(0,∞]T_{\max}:=T_{\max}(u_{0},v_{0})\in(0,\infty] such that (1.1) has a unique classical solution (u⁡(t,x,u0,v0),v⁡(t,x,u0,v0))(u(t,x;u_{0},v_{0}),v(t,x;u_{0},v_{0})) on (0,Tmax​(u0,v0))(0,T_{\max}(u_{0},v_{0})) with u⁡(0,x,u0,v0)=u0​(x)u(0,x;u_{0},v_{0})=u_{0}(x) and v⁡(0,x,u0,v0)=v0​(x)v(0,x;u_{0},v_{0})=v_{0}(x). In this subsection, we present two lemmas, which will be used frequently in the proofs of the main results. The first lemma is a Harnack type inequality, which is a generalization [13, Lemma 2.2]. The constants CC’s might depend on the parameters aa, bb, σ\sigma, τ\tau in the equation, as well as the dimension NN, without further notification.

2.3 Viscosity solutions

In this subsection, we briefly recall viscosity solutions. We refer readers to [6] for more details. This notion of solutions as well as the comparison principle will be one of the main tools we use in Section 5.2.

Consider the following parabolic type equation:

ut+F⁡(t,x,u,∇u,D2​u)=0.u_{t}+F(t,x,u,\nabla u,D^{2}u)=0. (2.11)

Let 𝒮N\mathcal{S}^{N} denote the set of N×NN\times N symmetric matrices with the spectral norm. We say that FF is uniformly elliptic, if there exists Λ>0\Lambda>0 such that for any positive semi-definite matrix P∈𝒮NP\in\mathcal{S}^{N}, and any (t,x,u,p,X)∈[0,∞)×ℝN×ℝ×ℝN×𝒮N(t,x,u,p,X)\in[0,\infty)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times{\mathbb{R}}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times\mathcal{S}^{N},

Λ​ Tr​(P)≤F⁡(t,x,u,p,X)−F⁡(t,x,u,p,X+P).\Lambda\text{ \rm Tr}(P)\leq F(t,x,u,p,X)-F(t,x,u,p,X+P).

We assume FF to be continuous and uniformly elliptic.

Now we recall the definition of viscosity solutions. Let Ω⊆ℝN\Omega\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}^{N} be open and T>0T>0.

  1. (i)

    We say that an upper semicontinuous (resp. lower semicontinuous) function u:(0,T)×Ω→ℝu:(0,T)\times\Omega\to\mathbb{R} is a (viscosity) subsolution (resp. (viscosity) supersolution) to (2.11) if the following holds: for any smooth function ϕ\phi in Ω\Omega such that u−ϕu-\phi has a local maximum (resp. minimum) at (t0,x0)∈(0,T)×Ω(t_{0},x_{0})\in(0,T)\times\Omega, we have

    ∂tu⁡(t0,x0)+F⁡(t0,x0,u⁡(t0,x0),∇ϕ​(t0,x0),D2​ϕ​(t0,x0))≤0\partial_{t}u(t_{0},x_{0})+{F}(t_{0},x_{0},u(t_{0},x_{0}),\nabla\phi(t_{0},x_{0}),D^{2}\phi(t_{0},x_{0}))\leq 0
    (resp. ​∂tu⁡(t0,x0)+F⁡(t0,x0,u⁡(t0,x0),∇ϕ​(t0,x0),D2​ϕ​(t0,x0))≥0).\left(\text{resp. }\partial_{t}u(t_{0},x_{0})+{F}(t_{0},x_{0},u(t_{0},x_{0}),\nabla\phi(t_{0},x_{0}),D^{2}\phi(t_{0},x_{0}))\geq 0\right).
  2. (ii)

    We say that a continuous function u:(0,T)×Ω→ℝu:(0,T)\times\Omega\to\mathbb{R} is a (viscosity) solution to (2.11) if it is both a subsolution and a supersolution.

It is easy to see that a classical solution is a viscosity solution.

For the purpose of the paper, we take

F⁡(t,x,u,∇u,D2​u)=−Δ​u+f⁡(t,x)⋅∇u+g⁡(t,x,u)F(t,x,u,\nabla u,D^{2}u)=-\Delta u+f(t,x)\cdot\nabla u+g(t,x,u) (2.12)

where f,gf,g are uniformly continuous and bounded functions. It is easy to check that the operator satisfies the condition (3.14) in [6]. Consequently, we have the following comparison principle.

Lemma 2.5.

Let T>0T>0 and let FF be given in (2.12). Let u+:(0,T)×ℝN→ℝu^{+}:(0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\to{\mathbb{R}} and u−:(0,T)×ℝN→ℝu^{-}:(0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\to{\mathbb{R}} be, respectively, a supersolution and a subsolution to (2.11). If u+​(0,⋅)≥u−​(0,⋅)u^{+}(0,\cdot)\geq u^{-}(0,\cdot) and inft∈(0,T)lim inf|x|→∞(u+​(t,x)−u−​(t,x))≥0\inf_{t\in(0,T)}\liminf_{|x|\to\infty}(u^{+}(t,x)-u^{-}(t,x))\geq 0, then

u+​(t,x)≥u−​(t,x) for all ​(t,x)∈(0,T)×ℝN.u^{+}(t,x)\geq u^{-}(t,x)\quad\text{ for all }(t,x)\in(0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{N}.

We refer readers to Sections 5D and 8 [6] for the proof and for more general cases.

In this subsection, we prove the convergence of globally defined bounded solutions with strictly positive initial data to the constant solution (ab,0)(\frac{a}{b},0). The result implies that there are no other positive stationary solutions (u⁡(x),v⁡(x))(u(x),v(x)) of (1.1) with infx∈ℝNu⁡(x)>0\inf_{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}u(x)>0 rather than (ab,0)(\frac{a}{b},0).

3 Lower bound of spreading speeds

In this section, we study the lower bounds of spreading speeds and prove Theorem 1.1. Throughout this section, we fix (u0,v0)∈X+×X1+(u_{0},v_{0})\in X^{+}\times X_{1}^{+} and suppose that (u⁡(t,x,u0,v0),v⁡(t,x,u0,v0))(u(t,x;u_{0},v_{0}),v(t,x;u_{0},v_{0})) is a globally defined bounded and non-negative solution of (1.1). We will often omit the dependence of constants on a,b,τa,b,\tau and NN.

3.1 Proof of Theorem 1.1(1)

The proof follows the line of those in [41], which studied (1.5). For us, nontrivial modifications are needed due to the difference of the system.

Let us fix any

0<c′<2​aand0<δ0<min⁡{1,2​a−c′,(a1/4​(2​N)−1)N}.0<{c^{\prime}}<2\sqrt{a}\quad\text{and}\quad 0<\delta_{0}<\min\left\{1,2\sqrt{a}-c^{\prime},(a^{1/4}(2N)^{-1})^{N}\right\}. (3.1)

lim inft→∞inf−2​a+δ0≤c≤2​a−δ0,ξ∈𝕊N−1(inf|x|≤R0u⁡(t,x+c​t​ξ,u0,v0))>0.\liminf_{t\to\infty}\inf_{-2\sqrt{a}+\delta_{0}\leq c\leq 2\sqrt{a}-\delta_{0},\xi\in\mathbb{S}^{N-1}}\left(\inf_{|x|\leq R_{0}}u(t,x+ct\xi;u_{0},v_{0})\right)>0. (3.2)

6 Numerical Simulation

In this section, we present the numerical results on the spreading speed of (1.1) in the one dimensional setting, i.e., N=1N=1, with the initial data having compact support. This investigation is accomplished through numerical simulations of the solutions to (1.16)+(1.17). All the numerical simulations were implemented using the Python programming language.

We start by defining the scheme for (1.16) and (1.17) as follows: We divide the space interval [−L,L][-L,L]  into MM subintervals with equal length and divide the time interval [0,T][0,T] into NN subintervals with equal length. Then the space step size is h=2​LMh=\frac{2L}{M} and  the time step size is τ∗=TN\tau^{*}=\frac{T}{N}. For simplicity, we denote the approximate value of u~​(tj,xi),v~​(tj,xi)\tilde{u}(t_{j},x_{i}),\tilde{v}(t_{j},x_{i}) by u~​(j,i),v~​(j,i)\tilde{u}(j,i),\tilde{v}(j,i) respectively, with tj=(j−1)​τ∗, 1≤j≤N+1t_{j}=(j-1)\tau^{*},\,1\leq j\leq N+1 and xi=−L+(i−1)​h, 1≤i≤M+1x_{i}=-L+(i-1)h,\,1\leq i\leq M+1. Using the central approximation for the spatial derivatives v~x​x​(tj,xi),v~x​(tj,xi)\tilde{v}_{xx}(t_{j},x_{i}),\tilde{v}_{x}(t_{j},x_{i}) and u~x​x​(tj,xi),u~x​(tj,xi)\tilde{u}_{xx}(t_{j},x_{i}),\tilde{u}_{x}(t_{j},x_{i}):

v~x​(tj,xi)\displaystyle\tilde{v}_{x}(t_{j},x_{i}) ≈v~​(j,i+1)−v~​(j,i−1)2​h,\displaystyle\approx\frac{\tilde{v}(j,i+1)-\tilde{v}(j,i-1)}{2h},
v~x​x​(tj,xi)\displaystyle\tilde{v}_{xx}(t_{j},x_{i}) ≈v~​(j,i−1)−2​v~​(j,i)+v~​(j,i+1)h2,\displaystyle\approx\frac{\tilde{v}(j,i-1)-2\tilde{v}(j,i)+\tilde{v}(j,i+1)}{h^{2}},
u~x​(tj,xi)\displaystyle\tilde{u}_{x}(t_{j},x_{i}) ≈u~​(j,i+1)−u~​(j,i−1)2​h,\displaystyle\approx\frac{\tilde{u}(j,i+1)-\tilde{u}(j,i-1)}{2h},
u~x​x​(tj,xi)\displaystyle\tilde{u}_{xx}(t_{j},x_{i}) ≈u~​(j,i−1)−2​u~​(j,i)+u~​(j,i+1)h2.\displaystyle\approx\frac{\tilde{u}(j,i-1)-2\tilde{u}(j,i)+\tilde{u}(j,i+1)}{h^{2}}.

The forward approximation of the time derivative yields

v~t​(tj,xi)≈v~​(j+1,i)−v~​(j,i)τ∗,u~t​(tj,xi)≈u~​(j+1,i)−u~​(j,i)τ∗.\displaystyle\tilde{v}_{t}(t_{j},x_{i})\approx\frac{\tilde{v}(j+1,i)-\tilde{v}(j,i)}{\tau^{*}},\qquad\tilde{u}_{t}(t_{j},x_{i})\approx\frac{\tilde{u}(j+1,i)-\tilde{u}(j,i)}{\tau^{*}}.

By the boundary conditions in (1.17), we set

u~​(j,1)=u~​(j,M+1)=0.\tilde{u}(j,1)=\tilde{u}(j,M+1)=0. (6.1)

Using the forward approximation for the Neumann boundary condition at −L-L and backward approximation at LL, we get

∂v~∂x​(tj,x1)≈v~​(j,2)−v~​(j,1)τ∗=0,∂v~∂x​(tj,xM+1)≈v~​(j,M+1)−v~​(j,M)τ∗=0,\frac{\partial\tilde{v}}{\partial x}(t_{j},x_{1})\approx\frac{\tilde{v}(j,2)-\tilde{v}(j,1)}{\tau^{*}}=0,\qquad\frac{\partial\tilde{v}}{\partial x}(t_{j},x_{M+1})\approx\frac{\tilde{v}(j,M+1)-\tilde{v}(j,M)}{\tau^{*}}=0,

and hence, we set

v⁡(j,2)=v⁡(j,1),v⁡(j,M+1)=v⁡(j,M).v(j,2)=v(j,1),\quad v(j,M+1)=v(j,M). (6.2)

The equation (1.16) can thus be discretized as: for 1≤j≤N,2≤i≤M1\leq j\leq N,2\leq i\leq M,

u~​(j+1,i)−u~​(j,i)τ∗=u~​(j,i−1)−2​u~​(j,i)+u~​(j,i+1)h2\displaystyle\frac{\tilde{u}(j+1,i)-\tilde{u}(j,i)}{\tau^{*}}=\frac{\tilde{u}(j,i-1)-2\tilde{u}(j,i)+\tilde{u}(j,i+1)}{h^{2}}

We use (6.1), (6.2), (6.3) and (6.4) in implementing the scheme on python, we apply the same space step size h=0.1h=0.1 and the same time step size τ∗=0.002.\tau^{*}=0.002. We carry out the numerical experiments for τ=1{\tau=1} and for different values of χ\chi and cc in subsections 6.1-6.3, and carry out the numerical experiments for different values of τ\tau, χ\chi, and cc in subsection 6.4. In all the simulations we take L=20L=20 and T=500T=500.

6.1 Numerical experiments with positive but not large χ\chi and observations

We carry out experiments with χ=1\chi=1, χ=1.25\chi=1.25 and χ=1.5\chi=1.5. For each of these χ\chi, we take cc to be of the following values: c=1,1.99,2.01,3c=1,1.99,2.01,3. Throughout this subsection, τ=1\tau=1. Figures 1 and 2 are the graphs of the uu-component of the numerical solutions of (1.16)+(1.17)+(1.19) with χ=1\chi=1, and c=1,1.99,2.01,3c=1,1.99,2.01,3 at some fixed times. Figure 3 are the graphs of the vv-component of the numerical solutions of (1.16)+(1.17)+(1.19) with χ=1\chi=1 and c=1,3c=1,3 at some fixed times.

We observe the following scenarios via the numerical simulations: The results of the numerical simulations with χ=1.25\chi=1.25 and χ=1.5\chi=1.5 are similar to those with χ=1\chi=1. The results show that when u~​(t,x)\tilde{u}(t,x) stays positive, v~​(t,x)→0\tilde{v}(t,x)\to 0 as t→∞t\to\infty, and when u~​(t,x)→0\tilde{u}(t,x)\to 0, v~​(t,x)\tilde{v}(t,x) stays positive as t→∞t\to\infty (we do not include all the graphs of the vv-component since we can infer the behavior of vv from uu). For 0<c<20<c<2, u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) stays positive, and for c>2c>2, u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) goes to 00 as t→∞t\to\infty, which indicates that chemotaxis with a positive but not large sensitivity coefficient χ\chi does not speed up the spreading.

6.2 Numerical experiments with positive and large χ\chi and observations

We carry out some numerical experiments with χ=2.5,5\chi=2.5,5 and χ=10\chi=10. For each of these χ\chi, we do simulations for the following values of cc; c=1,1.99,2.01,3c=1,1.99,2.01,3. Figures 4 and 5 are the graphs of the uu-component of the numerical solutions of (1.16)+(1.17)+(1.19) with χ=10\chi=10 and c=1,1.99,2.01,3c=1,1.99,2.01,3.

We observe that the results of numerical simulations with χ=2.5\chi=2.5 and χ=5\chi=5 are similar to those with χ=10\chi=10. We also observe that u~​(t,x)\tilde{u}(t,x) stays positive and v~​(t,x)→0\tilde{v}(t,x)\to 0 for c<2c<2 as well as for c=2.01c=2.01 as t→∞t\to\infty, which indicates that chemotaxis with positive large sensitivity coefficient χ\chi speeds up the spreading.

6.3 Numerical experiments with negative χ\chi and observations

We carry out numerical simulations with χ=−1\chi=-1 and χ=−10\chi=-10. For each of these χ\chi, we do simulations for the following values of cc, c=1,1.99,2.01,3c=1,1.99,2.01,3. Figures 6 and 7 are the graphs of the uu-component of the numerical solutions of (1.16)+(1.17)+(1.19) for χ=−1\chi=-1, and Figures 8 and 9 are the numerical solutions of (1.16)+(1.17)+(1.19) for χ=−10\chi=-10.

We observe that u~​(t,x)\tilde{u}(t,x) stays positive and v~​(t,x)→0\tilde{v}(t,x)\to 0 as t→∞t\to\infty for 0<c<20<c<2 and u~​(t,x)→0\tilde{u}(t,x)\to 0 and v~​(t,x)\tilde{v}(t,x) stays positive as t→∞t\to\infty, which indicates that chemotaxis with negative sensitivity coefficient or chemo-repeller does not speed up the spreading.

We give the following remarks on all experiments discussed in sections 6.1–6.3.

Remark 6.1.
  1. 1.

    The simulations indicate a critical point for χ\chi, i.e., there exists χ∗\chi^{*} between 1.5 and 1.9 such that for χ<χ∗\chi<\chi^{*}, the chemotaxis does not speed up the rate of spread, while for χ>χ∗\chi>\chi^{*}, The chemotaxis speeds up the spreading.

  2. 2.

    For c=3c=3, u⁡(t,x)→0u(t,x)\to 0 for all the values of χ\chi. This also supports the fact that cup∗<∞c^{*}_{\rm up}<\infty.

  3. 3.

    In the above numerical experiments, we used the same space step size h=0.1h=0.1 and the same time step size τ∗=0.002\tau^{*}=0.002 as they satisfy the numerical stability condition τ∗/h2<0.5\tau^{*}/h^{2}<0.5. We do not give an accuracy analysis of the simulations in this paper. To assess the reliability of the numerical results, we used different values of hh and τ∗\tau^{*} to simulate the spreading speed of the chemotaxis system in ℝ{\mathbb{R}}. We repeat the above experiments for h=0.1h=0.1 and τ∗=0.002,0.004\tau^{*}=0.002,0.004 and for τ∗=0.002\tau^{*}=0.002 and h=0.2h=0.2. The observed outcomes are close for the different values of hh and τ∗\tau^{*}.

6.4 Numerical Simulations for different τ\tau

We carry out some numerical experiments, to see the effect of τ\tau on the spreading speed. We choose τ=0.5,1,4\tau=0.5,1,4, and c=1,2.01,3c=1,2.01,3. The results of the 2D simulations of the uu-component are shown in subsections 6.4.1–6.4.3 for different time steps. In each of the images, (a) is the result for τ=0.5,\tau=0.5, (b) is the result for τ=1,\tau=1, and (c)(c) is for τ=4.\tau=4. All the images are for time t=0,5,10,20,500t=0,5,10,20,500 except for c=2.01,χ=1c=2.01,\chi=1, which is for time 0,5,20,500,1000.0,5,20,500,1000.

For c=2.01,c=2.01, we gave the result of the simulation with χ=1.9,5,10\chi=1.9,5,10. While for c=1c=1 and c=3,c=3, we show the result of the simulation for χ=1.9,5,10\chi=1.9,5,10

6.4.1 Results of simulation for c=1c=1

For c=1c=1, the solution all stays positive for all τ.\tau. This is expected from Theorem 1.1. The results of the simulations for χ=1.9,5,10\chi=1.9,5,10 are shown in Figures 10, 11 and 12.

6.4.2 Results of simulation for c=2.01c=2.01

The result of the simulations shows that the diffusion rate of vv has an effect on the spreading speed. We see that as τ\tau gets bigger, then uu goes to zero faster, see Figures 13–15. We also see that for large χ\chi there might be speed up for all the τ\tau, as seen for χ=5\chi=5 and χ=10\chi=10 in Figures 14 and 15.

6.4.3 Results of simulation for c=3c=3

We carry out the simulation for c=3c=3 and τ=0.5,1,4\tau=0.5,1,4. The results show that the solution goes to zero for large time and for all the τ\tau, see Figures 16–18.

Proof of Lemma 2.3.

By Lemma 2.2, we have

A=A⁡(χ,‖v0‖X1,‖u‖∞):=supt>1(‖∇v​(t,⋅)‖∞+‖Δ​v​(t,⋅)‖∞)<∞.A=A(\chi,\|v_{0}\|_{X_{1}},\|u\|_{\infty}):=\sup_{t>1}\left(\|\nabla v(t,\cdot)\|_{\infty}+\|\Delta v(t,\cdot)\|_{\infty}\right)<\infty.

We first prove (2.2). To this end, for given t0≥1t_{0}\geq 1, let t1:=t0−12t_{1}:=t_{0}-\frac{1}{2} and let u¯​(t,x)\bar{u}(t,x) be the solution of the equation

{u¯t=Δu¯−χ∇v(t,x)⋅∇u¯,(t,x)∈(t1,∞)×ℝN,u¯​(t1,⋅)=u⁡(t1,⋅),x∈ℝN.\begin{cases}\bar{u}_{t}=\Delta\bar{u}-\chi\nabla v(t,x)\cdot\nabla\bar{u},\qquad&(t,x)\in(t_{1},\infty)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\\ \bar{u}(t_{1},\cdot)=u(t_{1},\cdot),&x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}.\end{cases}

It follows from the comparison principle for parabolic equations that

0≤u¯​(t,x)≤‖u⁡(t1,⋅)‖∞≤‖u‖∞:=sups≥0‖u⁡(s,⋅)‖∞∀(t,x)∈(t1,∞)×ℝN.0\leq\bar{u}(t,x)\leq\|u(t_{1},\cdot)\|_{\infty}\leq\|u\|_{\infty}:=\sup_{s\geq 0}\|u(s,\cdot)\|_{\infty}\quad\forall\,(t,x)\in(t_{1},\infty)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{N}.

Let ψ⁡(t,x)\psi(t,x) and ϕ⁡(t,x)\phi(t,x) be defined by

ψ⁡(t,x)=min⁡{1,(a/b)1/σ/‖u‖∞}​e−|χ|​A​(t−t1)​u¯​(t,x)\psi(t,x)=\min\big\{1,({a}/{b})^{1/\sigma}/\|u\|_{\infty}\big\}\,e^{-|\chi|A(t-t_{1})}\,\bar{u}(t,x)

and

ϕ⁡(t,x)=e(a+A​|χ|)​(t−t1)​u¯​(t,x),\phi(t,x)=e^{(a+A|\chi|)(t-t_{1})}\,\bar{u}(t,x),

respectively. Then, we have for (t,x)∈(t1,∞)×ℝN(t,x)\in(t_{1},\infty)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{N},

ψt=−|χ|Aψ+Δψ−χ∇v⋅∇ψ≤Δψ−χ∇⋅(ψ∇v)≤Δψ−χ∇⋅(ψ∇v)+ψ(a−bψσ),\displaystyle\psi_{t}=-|\chi|A\psi+\Delta\psi-\chi\nabla v\cdot\nabla\psi\leq\Delta\psi-\chi\nabla\cdot(\psi\nabla v)\leq\Delta\psi-\chi\nabla\cdot(\psi\nabla v)+\psi(a-b\psi^{\sigma}),

and

ϕt\displaystyle\phi_{t} =(a+|χ|A)ϕ+Δϕ−χ∇v⋅∇ϕ≥Δϕ−χ∇⋅(ϕ∇v)+aϕ\displaystyle=(a+|\chi|A)\phi+\Delta\phi-\chi\nabla v\cdot\nabla\phi\geq\Delta\phi-\chi\nabla\cdot(\phi\nabla v)+a\phi
≥Δϕ−χ∇⋅(ϕ∇v)+ϕ(a−bϕσ).\displaystyle\geq\Delta\phi-\chi\nabla\cdot(\phi\nabla v)+\phi(a-b\phi^{\sigma}).

Since

ψ⁡(t1,⋅)≤ϕ⁡(t1,⋅)=u¯​(t1,⋅)=u⁡(t1,⋅),\psi(t_{1},\cdot)\leq\phi(t_{1},\cdot)=\bar{u}(t_{1},\cdot)=u(t_{1},\cdot),

the comparison principle yields

ψ⁡(t,⋅)≤u⁡(t,⋅)≤ϕ⁡(t,⋅)∀t≥t1.\psi(t,\cdot)\leq u(t,\cdot)\leq\phi(t,\cdot)\quad\forall\,t\geq t_{1}.

Note that

u¯​(t,x)=∫ℝNΓ⁡(t,t1,x,z)​u​(t1,z)​𝑑z,\bar{u}(t,x)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}\Gamma(t,t_{1},x,z)u(t_{1},z)dz,

where Γ⁡(t,t1,x,z)\Gamma(t,t_{1},x,z) is the fundamental solution of the equation

{Γt=ΔxΓ−χ∇xv⋅∇xΓ, for (t,x)∈(s,∞)×ℝN,Γ⁡(t=t1,t1,x,z)=δz​(x).\begin{cases}\Gamma_{t}=\Delta_{x}\Gamma-\chi\nabla_{x}v\cdot\nabla_{x}\Gamma,\qquad\qquad\text{ for }(t,x)\in(s,\infty)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\\ \Gamma(t=t_{1},t_{1},x,z)=\delta_{z}(x).\end{cases}

Hence

min⁡{1,(a/b)1/σ/‖u‖∞}​e−|χ|​A​(t−t1)​∫ℝNΓ⁡(t,t1,x,z)​u​(t1,z)​dz≤u⁡(s′,x)\displaystyle\min\left\{1,({a}/{b})^{1/\sigma}/\|u\|_{\infty}\right\}\,e^{-|\chi|A(t-t_{1})}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}\Gamma(t,t_{1},x,z)u(t_{1},z)dz\leq u(s^{\prime},x) (A.6)
≤e(a+A​|χ|)​(t−t1)∫ℝNΓ(t,t1,x,z)u(t1,z)dx∀t≥t1,x∈ℝN.\displaystyle\leq e^{(a+A|\chi|)(t-t_{1})}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}\Gamma(t,t_{1},x,z)u(t_{1},z)dx\quad\forall\,t\geq t_{1},\,\,x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}.

Let p>1p>1, qq be the conjugate exponent to pp and let α:=(1+p)/(2​p)\alpha:=(1+p)/(2p). From the proof of [13, (4.25)], for any fixed s0,R>0s_{0},R>0, there exists a constant C0>0C_{0}>0 depending only on s0s_{0}, RR, pp, AA, NN and an upper bound of |χ||\chi| such that

Γ​(t0,t1,x,z)α​p≤C0​Γ​(t,t1,y,z)​∀t∈[t0,t0+s0],|x−y|≤R,z∈ℝN.\Gamma(t_{0},t_{1},x,z)^{\alpha p}\leq C_{0}\,\Gamma(t,t_{1},y,z)\,\,\forall\,t\in[t_{0},t_{0}+s_{0}],\,\,|x-y|\leq R,\,\,z\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}. (A.7)

By [1, Theorem 10], there exists C1≥1C_{1}\geq 1, depending only AA, NN and an upper bound of |χ||\chi|, such that for any x,y∈ℝNx,y\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N} and 0≤s<t0\leq s<t with t−s≤12t-s\leq\frac{1}{2},

(C1(t−s)N/2)−1e−C1​|x−y|2t−s≤Γ(t,s,x,y)≤C1(t−s)−N/2e−|x−y|2C1​(t−s).({C_{1}(t-s)^{N/2}})^{-1}e^{-C_{1}\frac{|x-y|^{2}}{t-s}}\leq\Gamma(t,s,x,y)\leq{C_{1}}{(t-s)^{-N/2}}e^{-\frac{|x-y|^{2}}{C_{1}(t-s)}}.

∥Γ(t0,t1,x,⋅)1−α∥q≤C2∀x∈ℝN.\|\Gamma(t_{0},t_{1},x,\cdot)^{1-\alpha}\|_{q}\leq C_{2}\quad\forall\,x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}. (A.8)

By (A.6) and Hölder’s inequality, we have

u⁡(t0,x)\displaystyle u(t_{0},x) ≤e(a+A​|χ|)/2​∫ℝNΓ⁡(t0,t1,x,z)​u​(t1,z)​𝑑z\displaystyle\leq e^{(a+A|\chi|)/2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}\Gamma(t_{0},t_{1},x,z)\,u(t_{1},z)\,dz
≤e(a+A​|χ|)/2|u|∫ℝN∞1/q⁡(u⁡(t1,z)​Γ​(t0,t1,x,z)α​p)1/p​Γ​(t0,t1,x,z)(1−α)​𝑑z\displaystyle\leq e^{(a+A|\chi|)/2}\,\|u\|_{\infty}^{1/q}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}\left(u(t_{1},z)\,\Gamma(t_{0},t_{1},x,z)^{\alpha p}\right)^{1/p}\Gamma(t_{0},t_{1},x,z)^{(1-\alpha)}dz
≤e(a+A​|χ|)/2∥u∥∞1/q∥Γ(t0,t1,x,⋅)1−α∥q(∫ℝNu(t1,z)Γ(t0,t1,x,z)α​pdz)1/p.\displaystyle\leq e^{(a+A|\chi|)/2}\,\|u\|_{\infty}^{1/q}\,\|\Gamma(t_{0},t_{1},x,\cdot)^{1-\alpha}\|_{q}\left(\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}u(t_{1},z)\Gamma(t_{0},t_{1},x,z)^{\alpha p}dz\right)^{1/p}.

Using (A.7) and (A.8) yields for t∈[t0,t0+s0]t\in[t_{0},t_{0}+s_{0}],

u⁡(t0,x)\displaystyle u(t_{0},x) ≤C2​C01/p​e(a+A​|χ|)/2​‖u‖∞1/q​(∫ℝNu⁡(t1,z)​Γ​(t,t1,y,z)​𝑑z)1/p\displaystyle\leq C_{2}C_{0}^{1/p}e^{(a+A|\chi|)/2}\,\|u\|_{\infty}^{1/q}\,\left(\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}u(t_{1},z)\Gamma(t,t_{1},y,z)dz\right)^{1/p}
≤C2​C01/p​e(a+A​|χ|)/2+|χ|​A​(12+s0)/p​max⁡{‖u‖∞1/q,‖u‖∞​(b/a)1/(σ​p)}​u​(t,y)1/p,\displaystyle\leq C_{2}C_{0}^{1/p}e^{(a+A|\chi|)/2+|\chi|A(\frac{1}{2}+s_{0})/p}\max\left\{\|u\|_{\infty}^{1/q},\|u\|_{\infty}\left({b}/{a}\right)^{1/(\sigma p)}\right\}u(t,y)^{1/p},

where in the last inequality, we applied (A.6). We can conclude with (2.2).

Next, we prove (2.3). By a priori estimate for parabolic equations (see [32, Theorem 7.22]) and the anisotropic Sobolev embedding for q=N+3q=N+3 (see [7, Lemma A3]), there is C3=C3​(A,χ,R,N)>0C_{3}=C_{3}(A,\chi,R,N)>0 such that for any (t,x)∈(1,∞)×ℝn(t,x)\in(1,\infty)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{n},

|∇u​(t,x)|≤C3​(‖u‖Lq​([t−12,t]×BR​(x))+‖u⁡(a−b​u)‖Lq​([t−12,t]×BR​(x)))≤C3​‖u‖L∞​([t−12,t]×BR​(x))​(1+a+b​‖u‖∞).\begin{split}|\nabla u(t,x)|&\leq C_{3}\,\left(\|u\|_{L^{q}([t-\frac{1}{2},t]\times B_{R}(x))}+\|u(a-bu)\|_{L^{q}([t-\frac{1}{2},t]\times B_{R}(x))}\right)\\ &\leq C_{3}\,\|u\|_{L^{\infty}([t-\frac{1}{2},t]\times B_{R}(x))}\,(1+a+b\|u\|_{\infty}).\end{split}

By (2.2), for any p∈(1,∞)p\in(1,\infty), there exists a constant C>0C>0 that depends only on aa, bb, RR, pp, AA, NN, ‖u‖∞\|u\|_{\infty}, and an upper bound of |χ||\chi| such that

|∇u​(t,x)|≤C​u​(t,y)1/p|\nabla u(t,x)|\leq{C\,u(t,y)^{1/p}}

for all |x−y|≤R|x-y|\leq R, which proves (2.3). ∎
